case_info.scenario: A man aged 44 years was referred for progressive parkinsonism with poor levodopa response. His medical history comprised unexplained sensory hearing loss, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. At age 23 years, he had bilateral cataract surgery, and over the last 2 years, he developed worsening stiffness and walking difficulties with frequent falls. He reported features of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder, restless legs syndrome (RLS), visual daytime hallucinations, and rapid cognitive decline. He was given levodopa/benserazide (up to 200 mg/50 mg 4 times daily) without improvement on his Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale scores. Therefore, his dopaminergic medication was ceased. Family history was negative for movement or developmental disorders. His neurologic examination showed hypomimia, symmetrical bradykinesia, and rigidity of the extremities without tremors (Video). There was full range of eye movements with large-amplitude saccadic intrusions on smooth pursuit in all directions. Neuropsychological assessment revealed significant abnormalities in cognitive functioning, affecting verbal and nonverbal cognitive skills (ie, speed of information processing, visuospatial skills, verbal and visual memory loss, executive skills). Mini-Mental Status Examination score was 26 of 30 points. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing (ie, paraneoplastic antibodies Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2, Ma2, amphiphysin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, N-methyl-d-aspartic acid, LGI1, and Caspr2, 14-3-3 protein) were normal. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed mild frontal and parietal atrophy. An electroencephalogram demonstrated slowing in keeping with moderate generalized encephalopathy. Total-body positron emission tomography (PET) using fluorine 18 (18F) fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) as a tracer showed no FDG-avid lesions; however, a subsequent brain-specific FDG-PET/MRI revealed hypometabolism throughout the left cerebral hemisphere and crossed cerebellar diaschisis (Figure 1). As the patient’s cognitive function and parkinsonism had deteriorated rapidly, a brain biopsy of the left frontal cortex was done. Immunohistochemistry showed scattered globular inclusions consistent with Lewy bodies.

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

case_info.caption: A, Axial fluorine 18 (18F) fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) imaging shows reduced FDG uptake in the left frontal, temporal, and occipital lobes, as well as subtle hypometabolism in the left basal ganglia and left thalamus. case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). A man aged 44 years was referred for progressive parkinsonism with poor levodopa response. His medical history comprised unexplained sensory hearing loss, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. At age 23 years, he had bilateral cataract surgery, and over the last 2 years, he developed worsening stiffness and walking difficulties with frequent falls. He reported features of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder, restless legs syndrome (RLS), visual daytime hallucinations, and rapid cognitive decline. He was given levodopa/benserazide (up to 200 mg/50 mg 4 times daily) without improvement on his Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale scores. Therefore, his dopaminergic medication was ceased. Family history was negative for movement or developmental disorders. His neurologic examination showed hypomimia, symmetrical bradykinesia, and rigidity of the extremities without tremors (Video). There was full range of eye movements with large-amplitude saccadic intrusions on smooth pursuit in all directions. Neuropsychological assessment revealed significant abnormalities in cognitive functioning, affecting verbal and nonverbal cognitive skills (ie, speed of information processing, visuospatial skills, verbal and visual memory loss, executive skills). Mini-Mental Status Examination score was 26 of 30 points. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing (ie, paraneoplastic antibodies Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2, Ma2, amphiphysin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, N-methyl-d-aspartic acid, LGI1, and Caspr2, 14-3-3 protein) were normal. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed mild frontal and parietal atrophy. An electroencephalogram demonstrated slowing in keeping with moderate generalized encephalopathy. Total-body positron emission tomography (PET) using fluorine 18 (18F) fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) as a tracer showed no FDG-avid lesions; however, a subsequent brain-specific FDG-PET/MRI revealed hypometabolism throughout the left cerebral hemisphere and crossed cerebellar diaschisis (Figure 1). As the patient’s cognitive function and parkinsonism had deteriorated rapidly, a brain biopsy of the left frontal cortex was done. Immunohistochemistry showed scattered globular inclusions consistent with Lewy bodies.

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

case_info.scenario: A man aged 44 years was referred for progressive parkinsonism with poor levodopa response. His medical history comprised unexplained sensory hearing loss, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. At age 23 years, he had bilateral cataract surgery, and over the last 2 years, he developed worsening stiffness and walking difficulties with frequent falls. He reported features of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder, restless legs syndrome (RLS), visual daytime hallucinations, and rapid cognitive decline. He was given levodopa/benserazide (up to 200 mg/50 mg 4 times daily) without improvement on his Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale scores. Therefore, his dopaminergic medication was ceased. Family history was negative for movement or developmental disorders. His neurologic examination showed hypomimia, symmetrical bradykinesia, and rigidity of the extremities without tremors (Video). There was full range of eye movements with large-amplitude saccadic intrusions on smooth pursuit in all directions. Neuropsychological assessment revealed significant abnormalities in cognitive functioning, affecting verbal and nonverbal cognitive skills (ie, speed of information processing, visuospatial skills, verbal and visual memory loss, executive skills). Mini-Mental Status Examination score was 26 of 30 points. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing (ie, paraneoplastic antibodies Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2, Ma2, amphiphysin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, N-methyl-d-aspartic acid, LGI1, and Caspr2, 14-3-3 protein) were normal. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed mild frontal and parietal atrophy. An electroencephalogram demonstrated slowing in keeping with moderate generalized encephalopathy. Total-body positron emission tomography (PET) using fluorine 18 (18F) fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) as a tracer showed no FDG-avid lesions; however, a subsequent brain-specific FDG-PET/MRI revealed hypometabolism throughout the left cerebral hemisphere and crossed cerebellar diaschisis (Figure 1). As the patient’s cognitive function and parkinsonism had deteriorated rapidly, a brain biopsy of the left frontal cortex was done. Immunohistochemistry showed scattered globular inclusions consistent with Lewy bodies.

case_info.caption: A, Axial fluorine 18 (18F) fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) imaging shows reduced FDG uptake in the left frontal, temporal, and occipital lobes, as well as subtle hypometabolism in the left basal ganglia and left thalamus. B, Crossed cerebellar diaschisis as a result of contralateral supratentorial asymmetry is seen in the coronal plane.
case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy. This was confirmed by the histopathological finding of Lewy bodies (Figure 2). In patients with early-onset parkinsonism (<50 years), genetic variants should be considered, even with a negative family history. Genetic screening in this patient revealed a novel homozygous variant (c.189dupA [p. Glu64Argfs*5]) within the DJ-1 protein of thePARK7gene, confirming autosomal-recessive parkinsonism. PARK7is one of the rare causative genes for early-onset Parkinson disease (frequency of 1%-2%).1The DJ-1 protein is expressed in almost all cells (eg, neurons and glial cells) and protects against oxidative stress by various mechanisms.2In vitro studies have shown that DJ-1 functions as a chaperone protein, modulating α-synuclein oligomerization and cytotoxicity. Absence of DJ-1 inPARK7gene variants causes a dysregulation in the brain, resulting in misfolding and aggregation.3The increased prevalence of mitochondrial features in patients with Lewy body pathology highlights the role ofPARK7gene variants in mitochondrial homeostasis.4Although the exact mechanism is still unclear, in vivo studies have shown that DJ-1 specifically acts on mitochondrial complex I, resulting in oxidative stress resistance.5 Typically, patients withPARK7gene variants have phenotypes similar to idiopathic Parkinson disease, although more complex syndromes with features of anterior horn cell disorders have been described. A recent literature review suggests that a triad of early-onset Parkinson disease, cataracts, and sensorineural hearing loss may be specific for DJ-1/PARK7; however, the phenotypic spectrum is still expanding.6 This patient’s motor and cognitive decline have gradually progressed, and he required a wheelchair at age 46 years (<5 years after symptom onset). In this period, he was again given levodopa/benserazide (maximum 200 mg/50 mg given 3 times daily) and a dopamine agonist (rotigotine patch, maximum 6 mg/24 hours); both were not beneficial and were discontinued. At 48 years of age, he was diagnosed with Parkinson disease dementia and is currently being treated with rivastigmine.

A man aged 44 years was referred for progressive parkinsonism with poor levodopa response. His medical history comprised unexplained sensory hearing loss, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. At age 23 years, he had bilateral cataract surgery, and over the last 2 years, he developed worsening stiffness and walking difficulties with frequent falls. He reported features of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder, restless legs syndrome (RLS), visual daytime hallucinations, and rapid cognitive decline. He was given levodopa/benserazide (up to 200 mg/50 mg 4 times daily) without improvement on his Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale scores. Therefore, his dopaminergic medication was ceased. Family history was negative for movement or developmental disorders. His neurologic examination showed hypomimia, symmetrical bradykinesia, and rigidity of the extremities without tremors (Video). There was full range of eye movements with large-amplitude saccadic intrusions on smooth pursuit in all directions. Neuropsychological assessment revealed significant abnormalities in cognitive functioning, affecting verbal and nonverbal cognitive skills (ie, speed of information processing, visuospatial skills, verbal and visual memory loss, executive skills). 3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: In patients with relative subacute onset of cognitive decline and movement disorders, treatable causes must be ruled out. In this patient, central nervous system infection was unlikely owing to normal laboratory and cerebral spinal fluid testing. Paraneoplastic antibody screening was negative, with no malignancies on total-body PET. Newer antibodies against the glycine receptor (GlyR) and immunoglobulinlike cell adhesion molecule 5 (IgLON5) have been discovered that mimic atypical parkinsonian syndromes. Anti-GlyR antibodies are typically associated with stiff-person syndromes or progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Patients with IgLON5 antibodies develop a sleep disorder with parasomnia and/or breathing difficulty with bulbar symptoms, gait abnormalities, oculomotor problems, chorea, and cognitive decline. Although untreatable, the patient’s symptoms, disease course, and abnormal electroencephalogram could indicate Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, but one would expect MRI changes and 14-3-3 protein. Symmetrical parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, early falls, rapid cognitive decline, and brain hypometabolism may raise the suspicion of a tauopathy, eg, progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal degeneration. However, preserved vertical gaze, presence of rapid eye movement–sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and very early onset of symptoms are atypical, and tauopathies were ruled out after brain biopsy. The history of cataracts, hearing loss, osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia, made us consider mitochondrial diseases, but screening (eg, mitochondrial DNA testing) was negative. Typical nonmotor features (RBD, restless legs syndrome, visual daytime hallucinations) are a strong indicator for an α-synucleinopathy.
